name: Prize crossword No 22,607
preamble: 1 across is the keyword, whence are derived four unclued theme words: 12, 27, 53 and 55. These in turn each have four variations, each relating in the same way to its theme, plus a fifth relating differently. Clues to the variations are often incomplete.

clue.text: Set in line of battle, perhaps: so 5 down consulted higher authority?

definitions.text: Set in line of battle, perhaps

blocks.clueFragment: Set in line of battle, perhaps
blocks.note: first meaning: drawn up in formation, as troops are before a fight
second meaning, split in two: a war correspondent telephoned his editor, the higher authority

explanation.surface: Troops drawn up for battle, while the reporter at the front phones home for orders.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as RANG ED: the war correspondent (5 down) rang the Ed, his editor. The preamble makes this the keyword whose letters yield the four theme words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ranged means arranged in rows or ranks, as an army is placed in its battle line.

clue.text: A candle or candles I need to play

indicators.note: read as its twin 'knead', it asks for the letters to be worked like dough into a new shape

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: Someone needs a candle or two in order to put on a show.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is the whole run of words before 'need', seventeen letters in all. Arsenic and Old Lace is Joseph Kesselring's black comedy about two poisoning aunts.
explanation.definitionFit: Kesselring's 1939 stage comedy, later filmed with Cary Grant, is a famous theatrical work.

definitions.note: a phrase of purpose standing for a noun: one who gums

blocks.note: first meaning: a Conservative cabinet minister of the 1980s and 1990s, later Lord Deben
second meaning: a person or device that applies glue

explanation.surface: A retired politician hired to keep things together.
explanation.walkthrough: John Selwyn Gummer was a British Conservative minister, later Lord Deben; the second half reads the surname as an ordinary word for someone who applies adhesive.
explanation.definitionFit: Gum is glue, so a gummer is literally whoever or whatever applies adhesive to fix items together.

clue.text: Girl in frenzied ride for love

indicators.note: anything frenzied is wild and disordered, so its letters lose their order
one thing sitting in another means it is placed inside it

blocks.note: a girl's name
taken as written
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A girl caught up in a wild ride, all for love.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue has no definition: per the preamble this is a variation on 12 (GRANDE), since Rio de Janeiro, like Rio Grande, follows Rio.
explanation.definitionFit: Rio de Janeiro is the Brazilian city, so these words complete a name beginning with Rio, the shared theme for 12.

definitions.note: describes rose water rather than defining the bare word

blocks.note: first meaning: the clarity of a gem
second meaning: what follows ROSE (48) in the scented liquid

explanation.surface: Something of fine quality, scented with roses.
explanation.walkthrough: 48 is ROSE, and rose water is scented; the preamble makes WATER one of the variations on GARDEN (water garden).
explanation.definitionFit: Jewellers grade diamonds by their water, their transparency and lustre, so a stone of the first water is top grade.

clue.text: Bad prose among trite stuff in the Guardian, with little time for our man at the front?

indicators.note: something bad is spoilt or wrong, so these letters are rearranged
to be among things is to sit in their midst, so one piece goes inside
being in something means lying within it, so a piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a warden is a guardian or keeper
corn is hackneyed, sentimental material
taken as written
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A complaint about poor, clichéd writing in the Guardian newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Guardian' looks like the newspaper but is a warden; the reshuffled prose sits inside corn, which sits inside the warden, and T follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper calls its frontline reporter 'our man', and a journalist reporting from a battle zone is a war correspondent.

clue.text: The only cog to work the machines?

indicators.note: working material means kneading or shaping it, so the letters get remade

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A lone gear wheel trying to keep a whole factory running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' belongs to the fodder; the cog and the machines make one picture, which is why the definition carries a question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: Technology is the collective term for practical machinery, devices and engineering systems.

blocks.note: first meaning: a stick of hard seaside sweet
second meaning: to sway to and fro

explanation.walkthrough: Rock is a British seaside sweet sold in sticks with a town's name running through it. The preamble makes it a variation on GARDEN (rock garden).
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names a cylindrical stick of candy; the verb means sway gently back and forth.

blocks.note: the adjective meaning notable or striking
the bracketed word completes a stock phrase using the adjective, confirming its sense

explanation.walkthrough: A signal success is a conspicuous one. The preamble makes this word a variation on DANGER (danger signal).
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective the word means conspicuous or remarkable, used chiefly in set phrases about achievements.

clue.text: Deer drinking 30 down in spite of bacterium

indicators.note: whatever drinks takes something into itself, so it encloses another piece
being in something means lying inside it, so this piece is enclosed

blocks.note: taken as written
a roe is a small deer
30 down is TEA, and cha is British slang for tea

explanation.surface: A deer that keeps drinking tea despite carrying a bacterium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In spite of' reads as one phrase, but 'spite' supplies the outer letters. RIO also hides here in shuffled form, as 37 notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirochaetes are spiral-shaped bacteria, including the organisms responsible for syphilis and Lyme disease.

blocks.note: Goa is a state on India's west coast
a head is a leader

explanation.surface: A forward-thinking politician leading an Indian state.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists leader before state, but the answer reads the state first; 'for' tells you the leader stands in for something in the state's name, so ignore it as order.
explanation.definitionFit: Go-ahead describes someone enterprising and keen on new ideas, which is what progressive means.

clue.text: I intend rising in the motoring organisation - bloodlessly?

definitions.note: an adverb clueing a noun: anaemia is the condition of being bloodless

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means read from the bottom upward
placing one thing in another puts it inside

blocks.note: to intend is to mean
the AA is the Automobile Association, Britain's main motoring breakdown club

explanation.surface: Someone proposes to climb within the AA, but without spilling blood.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose, hence the question mark: the answer is the condition, the clue gives its manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Anaemia is a deficiency of red blood cells or haemoglobin, leaving a person pale and seemingly drained.

clue.text: Choirboy gets it in the neck

blocks.clueFragment: Choirboy gets it in the neck
blocks.note: surface reading: a chorister being punished or scolded
setter's reading: the pleated frill a chorister wears round the throat

explanation.walkthrough: 'Gets it in the neck' is an idiom for being punished, but here it is literal: the collar a cathedral chorister wears. The preamble makes this a variation on GANDER, since the word is also a male bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A ruff is a stiff pleated collar; the same word names a wading bird whose male shows a frilled neck.

blocks.note: unclued; the preamble derives it from the keyword at 1 across

explanation.surface: A list of cross-references, as if the entry were a catalogue of musical variations.
explanation.walkthrough: This is the keyword RANGED rearranged. Each listed variation follows RIO: Rio de Janeiro, Rio Ferdinand, Rio Bravo, Rio Tinto, while RIO itself (37) goes before GRANDE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rio Grande is the river forming much of the border between the United States and Mexico.

clue.text: Old city, with it, to get a degree on 1st of June or plough

indicators.note: first of a word means only its opening letter is kept

blocks.note: Ur was an ancient city of Mesopotamia
it means sex appeal, abbreviated SA
an MA is a Master of Arts degree
the month's opening letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ancient city graduating someone, then a choice between June and ploughing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' as sex appeal, SA, is a crossword staple. 'Plough' is the last word, so it is the definition, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: The Plough is the British name for seven bright stars forming part of the Great Bear constellation.

clue.text: Many at start of play will bloom in the desert

definitions.note: a clause describing the plants rather than a noun

blocks.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, taken as many
Act I opens a play

explanation.surface: Lots of flowers appearing as the curtain rises on a desert play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Start of play' tempts you to take a single letter P, but it is the whole first act, ACT I.
explanation.definitionFit: Cacti are succulent plants native to arid regions that produce showy flowers after rain.

definitions.note: two first names sharing this surname, not a synonym

blocks.note: AD, Anno Domini, marks the modern era
an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A redbreast singing a fresh melody.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Red Robin' looks like the bird, but each word is a first name: Red Adair the oil-well firefighter and Robin Adair, the Irish song.
explanation.definitionFit: Both famous bearers share the surname: the American firefighter Red Adair and the ballad hero Robin Adair.

clue.text: Dancer from the fen dancing with Tony

indicators.note: letters that dance move about and change places

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dancer from the fenlands partnering a man called Tony.
explanation.walkthrough: Margot Fonteyn was the great English prima ballerina, famous for her partnership with Nureyev.
explanation.definitionFit: Dame Margot Fonteyn was the celebrated principal ballerina of Britain's Royal Ballet.

clue.text: From Cameroon there comes a camel

indicators.note: taking something from a phrase means lifting letters already inside it

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: An exotic animal shipped out of West Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Oont is Anglo-Indian slang for a camel, familiar from Kipling.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, from Hindi, was soldiers' slang in British India for the dromedary.

clue.text: Financier's complaint about marshal being given his head

indicators.note: to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes around the others

blocks.note: a moan is a complaint
Michel Ney was one of Napoleon's marshals
'his' refers to the marshal, who is given his own initial letter, M

explanation.surface: A banker grumbling about a military officer being promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being given his head' sounds like being allowed free rein, but the marshal gains his own first letter. Both halves also follow DANGER in the theme: danger money, danger man.
explanation.definitionFit: A money man is a backer or person who handles the finances of a venture.

clue.text: Kipling's 13 devours teetotal son of Blair, following 5 across to a Boney conclusion

indicators.note: to devour is to swallow whole, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: 13 is URSA MAJOR, the Great Bear, and Kipling's bear in The Jungle Book is Baloo
TT is the abbreviation for teetotal
Leo Blair was born to Tony Blair while he was Prime Minister
f. is the abbreviation for following
the answer to 5 across

explanation.surface: A literary bear swallowing the Prime Minister's sober son before a soggy, bony ending.
explanation.walkthrough: Boney was the British nickname for Napoleon. Kipling's bear has to be split, its first two letters before and last three after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon's final defeat in 1815 ended his career, the conclusion of Boney's story.

blocks.note: surface reading: someone keeping watch on a weaver's shuttle or a space shuttle
setter's reading: the word that comes next in the name of the feathered badminton missile

explanation.walkthrough: The word follows 'shuttle' to make shuttlecock. The preamble makes it a variation on GANDER: like a gander, it is a male bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A cock is a male fowl, and it completes the name of the shuttlecock hit in badminton.

definitions.note: the phrase leaves 'nut', and the answer is a kind of nut

blocks.note: first meaning: a sturdy short-legged riding horse
second meaning: take 'chest' off 'chestnut' and a nut remains, here a hazelnut

explanation.surface: A conker tree stripped of its first syllable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horse chestnut' looks like the tree; split it into a horse and a nut. The preamble makes this a variation on GANDER, as it is also a male swan.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a stocky riding horse and also the large hazelnut known as a cobnut.

indicators.note: something following comes after, so the first piece read goes second

blocks.note: Diana, Princess of Wales, was known as Di
or introduces an alternative

explanation.surface: A different set of believers lining up behind a royal Christian.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer, but it is a first name: the French fashion designer Christian Dior.
explanation.definitionFit: Christian is the forename of the Paris couturier who launched the New Look in 1947.

blocks.note: first meaning: Cary Grant was born Archibald Alexander with this surname
a bonus reference to Bernard, the English studio potter of this surname
second meaning: a vessel through which liquid is filtered

explanation.surface: Applying for a subsidy to buy a coffee maker for a pottery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' looks like money but is the film star. A leach is a tub for percolating water through ash; Bernard Leach was the father of British studio pottery.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to Cary Grant at birth, and as a noun it names a filtering vessel.

definitions.note: a phrase standing for a famous seafarer

blocks.note: first meaning: the man who famously finished his game of bowls on Plymouth Hoe as the Armada approached
second meaning: the Elizabethan admiral who sailed round the world

explanation.surface: A cricketer, or a hat, adrift on the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowler' suggests cricket or a hat; the game is bowls. The preamble makes this a variation on GANDER, since a drake is a male duck.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Francis Drake was both the legendary bowls player of 1588 and England's great Elizabethan sea captain.

indicators.note: something off has gone bad or wrong, so its letters are disordered

blocks.note: a net catches things
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fielder who has dropped a catch and been reprieved.
explanation.walkthrough: No definition: 55 calls this 'this 24', from Hotspur's line in Henry IV Part 1, 'out of this nettle, danger, we pluck this flower, safety'.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Hotspur pairs this stinging plant with danger, the theme word at 55 across.

clue.text: Streamers for knights errant on red slab

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so the letters stray from their order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: Pennants for wandering knights laid out on a red stone slab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knights errant' reads as a set phrase, but 'errant' belongs to the wordplay and 'knights' to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Banderols are long narrow flags or pennons, flown from the lance of a mounted knight.

definitions.note: completes the phrase: becomes betrothed with a ring

blocks.note: first meaning: a telephone line becomes occupied
second meaning: a couple agree to marry, marked with a ring

explanation.walkthrough: The ring suggests a phone call, which fits the busy line too; both meanings share the one phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Engaged is the British term for a busy phone line, and also means promised in marriage.

blocks.note: unclued; the preamble derives it from the keyword at 1 across

explanation.surface: A list of cross-references, as if the entry were a catalogue of musical variations.
explanation.walkthrough: The keyword rearranged. The variations RUFF, COCK, COB and DRAKE are each a male bird, as a gander is a male goose; 'commonly butchers' is a look, as in 'take a gander'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gander is a male goose, and in slang a gander is also a quick look.

indicators.note: things that turn out unfortunately go wrong, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: every letter of these words is used

explanation.surface: A reconnaissance at dusk goes badly and someone gets eaten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Swallowed' looks like eating, but it means believed, as in swallowing a story.
explanation.definitionFit: To swallow a tale is to accept it as true, so a story that got swallowed was believed.

definitions.note: a position in a title rather than a synonym

blocks.note: first meaning: a dung beetle, or any droning insect
second meaning: 20 across in French is coq

explanation.surface: An insect trailing after a French cockerel.
explanation.walkthrough: D'OR, 'of gold', follows COQ in the opera title The Golden Cockerel.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an old name for a dung beetle that flies with a loud hum.

clue.text: Interfering old woman to make love and to draw fish

definitions.note: a purpose phrase describing the lure

blocks.note: an old trout is a fussy, meddlesome old woman
to spoon is an old word for to court or canoodle

explanation.surface: A meddling old lady gets amorous and goes fishing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old trout' is British slang for a cantankerous old woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A trout-spoon is a small spoon-shaped metal lure that spins in the water to attract trout.

definitions.note: a past participle standing for a noun: something that is drunk

indicators.note: the sound of something is how it is spoken, not how it is written

blocks.note: the twentieth letter of the alphabet, as it is spoken

explanation.surface: A letter's noise disappearing down someone's throat.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose because this is a theme variation: tea garden is one of the four GARDEN variations.
explanation.definitionFit: Tea is a drink, and a drink is what gets swallowed down.

clue.text: Colleague of Blair (Tony) out of bed before queen and emperor

indicators.note: to get out of something is to leave it, so those letters are dropped
coming before means placed ahead in the order

blocks.note: the surname of Blair's Deputy Prime Minister, whose first name is used at the end
a cot is a small bed
ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's cipher

explanation.surface: A cabinet minister rising before the Queen and an emperor.
explanation.walkthrough: Blair's colleague is John Prescott, and both his names are used: the surname loses its bed and the first name goes to the end. The bracketed Tony stops you thinking of Leo Blair from 19.
explanation.definitionFit: Prester John was a legendary Christian priest-king believed in medieval Europe to rule a far eastern realm.

clue.text: 0 per cent finance for Peter Pan?

definitions.note: his home, not the boy himself

blocks.note: first meaning: British slang for hire purchase, with a wink at a deal where you pay nothing
second meaning: the land where the boy who never grew up lives

explanation.surface: An interest-free loan for the boy who wouldn't grow up.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain buying on the never-never means hire purchase, paying in instalments. Peter Pan lives in the Never Never Land.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang term names credit by instalments and also echoes Barrie's island of lost boys.

clue.text: A fellow receiving a point at first, as is fitting

blocks.note: taken as written
a don is a university fellow
taken as written
PT is the abbreviation for point
taken as written
first is one, the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A man getting a point in first, as is only proper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At first' looks like an instruction to take initial letters, but AT and first (I) are separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A fitting, like an adaptation, is an adjustment made so something suits its purpose.

clue.text: Dead twice? He left off, being mentally confused

indicators.note: something off is wrong or awry, so the letters fall out of order

blocks.note: the word written out two times
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: Someone who has died twice and then walked off would be thoroughly bewildered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left off' reads as stopped, but 'left' gives L and 'off' rearranges everything.
explanation.definitionFit: Addled means muddled, so an addle-headed person is confused and unable to think clearly.

clue.text: One that fought with Old Pretender for more than a sonnet?

definitions.text: One that fought with Old Pretender

blocks.clueFragment: One that fought with Old Pretender
blocks.note: first meaning: a supporter of the 1715 Jacobite rising
second meaning: a poem one line longer than the usual fourteen

explanation.surface: A Jacobite soldier with poetic ambitions beyond the sonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: The Old Pretender was James Stuart, whose 1715 rising is called 'the Fifteen'. A sonnet has fourteen lines.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means a rebel of 1715 and also a fifteen-line poem, one more than a sonnet.

definitions.note: names a king by his realm

blocks.note: first meaning: Rio, the England centre-back of the 2000s
second meaning: the king who with Isabella united Spain

explanation.walkthrough: The footballer is Rio Ferdinand, so this is a GRANDE variation following RIO. Ferdinand II of Aragon married Isabella of Castile.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to the English defender Rio and to the fifteenth-century Spanish monarch.

clue.text: 5 across found variously in 4, 8 down and 51

definitions.note: Spanish for river, a body of water

indicators.note: something found has been discovered lying within, so the letters are already present

blocks.note: the letters run inside this word, after its first two
the same three letters, in other orders, also sit inside these answers

explanation.surface: Water turning up in different forms across several places.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Variously' looks like the instruction to shuffle, but it is the hiding place. The same letters lurk in DE JANEIRO, SPIROCHAETE and ORIBI in varying order. 12 says RIO goes 'before all' the GRANDE variations.
explanation.definitionFit: Rio is the Spanish and Portuguese word for river, so a stand-in for water.

clue.text: It isn't extra for a skin transplant

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A skin graft offered at no additional cost.
explanation.walkthrough: There is no separate signal for the hidden word; the skin transplant itself is the hiding place. 'Extra' here is the Latin prefix meaning outside.
explanation.definitionFit: Intra and extra are opposed Latin prefixes, inside versus outside, so one is precisely not the other.

clue.text: Take liquid in clouds that don't begin to exist

indicators.note: not beginning means the opening letter is missing

blocks.note: nimbi is the plural of nimbus, a rain cloud
to be is to exist

explanation.surface: Soaking up water in clouds that have no beginning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take liquid in clouds' tempts you to read rain; the definition stops at 'in'.
explanation.definitionFit: To imbibe is to drink, literally to absorb fluid into the body.

clue.text: Russian girl with tales of French comedian?

ana is a collection of anecdotes or sayings about a person

explanation.walkthrough: Ana as a suffix makes 'Tatiana' read as tales of Tati, the question mark admitting the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: Tatiana is a common Russian woman's name, famous as the heroine of Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.

definitions.note: a town described by its county

blocks.note: first meaning: the child author of The Young Visiters, written aged nine
second meaning: a market town in Kent, the county in south-east England

explanation.walkthrough: 'Daisy' looks like a flower, but she is the writer Daisy Ashford; Kent is a county in south-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the young Victorian novelist is also the name of a Kentish town on the Channel rail line.

blocks.note: a ton is a unit of weight
a figure going up is increasing

explanation.surface: Mass growing as velocity rises, as in physics.
explanation.walkthrough: Ton-up is British slang for doing a hundred miles an hour, especially on a motorbike; a ton is also slang for a hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: A ton-up is a speed of one hundred miles per hour, the goal of 1960s rockers.

blocks.note: ac is the abbreviation for account, a bill
re means concerning, as in a letter heading

explanation.surface: A piece of legislation about property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bill' looks like a law in Parliament, but it is an account.
explanation.definitionFit: An acre is a measured area of ground, and acres are a figurative word for estate or territory.

clue.text: A right to travel by ship

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
to go is to travel

explanation.surface: Someone claiming the entitlement to journey by sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By ship' sounds like a mode of transport; the ship is the definition itself.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo is the vessel in Greek myth that carried Jason and the Argonauts to find the Golden Fleece.

blocks.note: surface reading: divided out between people
setter's reading: a plain adjective, held by all jointly, which also does duty in the theme

explanation.walkthrough: A plain one-word clue: it feeds the theme, as 53 lists it as 'and/or 44' (common or garden) and 27 uses it in '44-ly 45', commonly called a butcher's.
explanation.definitionFit: Something common belongs to or is used jointly by a group, like a village green.

second meaning: the tradesmen or shops you go to for meat

explanation.definitionFit: The rhyming-slang term means a glance, and the plural noun names meat traders.

definitions.note: the phrase needs 'to' added, as in 'with a view to'

blocks.note: first meaning: sorted, neatly sequenced
second meaning: for the purpose of, as when followed by 'to'

explanation.walkthrough: 'With a view' suggests a room with scenery; it is the purposive phrase 'with a view to', just as 'in order to'.

clue.text: The 30 down one is one, the 7 one isn't

definitions.note: an adjective phrase for a verb or noun meaning lean

explanation.definitionFit: A table can be a tabulated register, and a ship that leans sideways is said to have a tilt.

blocks.note: first meaning: a cry of well done
second meaning: a hired killer, from the Italian

indicators.note: being about something means going round it, so one piece encloses another

a rib is a bone

explanation.walkthrough: 'Summons' looks like a court order, but it is the attention-getting call 'oi'.
explanation.definitionFit: The oribi is a small, slender antelope of the African savannah.

clue.text: The staff of an organisation are among the dregs -- they produce heavy stuff

admin is the administrative staff

explanation.walkthrough: 'Heavy stuff' sounds like dull reading; it is literal, a dense metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Lead is notoriously heavy, and lead mines extract it from the ground.

blocks.note: unclued; the preamble derives it from the keyword at 1 across

explanation.walkthrough: The keyword rearranged. Each variation goes before it: water garden, rock garden, tea garden, rose garden; 44 links differently, as 'common or garden'.
explanation.definitionFit: A garden is a cultivated plot of ground for growing flowers, fruit or vegetables.

clue.text: Model keen on half Venetian painter

explanation.definitionFit: The first five letters of the sixteenth-century Venetian master's name supply exactly half of it.
